title: N+1 query problem
short: One parent query plus one query per accessed association.
answer: Fix with fetch joins, EntityGraphs, batch fetching or projections.
code: SELECT o FROM Order o JOIN FETCH o.customer
interview: One parent query plus one query per accessed association.

title: Database sharding
short: Partition data across nodes using a shard key.
answer: A good key distributes load and supports common access patterns; cross-shard queries add complexity.
code: user_id hash -> shard
interview: Partition data across nodes using a shard key.

title: Read replicas vs sharding
short: Replicas scale reads; sharding partitions data to scale capacity/write load.
answer: Replicas may lag; sharding complicates queries and rebalancing.
code:
Primary -> replicas
Shard A/B/C
interview: Replicas scale reads; sharding partitions data to scale capacity/write load.

title: Primary key
short: A primary key uniquely identifies rows and cannot be null.
answer: A table has one primary-key constraint, possibly composite.
code: CREATE TABLE student(id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,name VARCHAR(100));
interview: A primary key uniquely identifies rows and cannot be null.

title: Primary vs unique key
short: Both enforce uniqueness; a table has one primary key and can have multiple unique constraints.
answer: Primary key columns are non-null. NULL semantics for unique constraints vary by DB.
code: ALTER TABLE student ADD CONSTRAINT uq_email UNIQUE(email);
interview: Both enforce uniqueness; a table has one primary key and can have multiple unique constraints.

title: Foreign key
short: A foreign key enforces referential integrity.
answer: It ensures references point to valid parent keys subject to null and action semantics.
code: FOREIGN KEY(customer_id) REFERENCES customer(id)
interview: A foreign key enforces referential integrity.

title: Normalization
short: Normalization reduces redundant facts and update anomalies.
answer: Normal forms improve integrity; intentional denormalization can help performance.
code:
Customer(id,name)
Order(id,customer_id,...)
interview: Normalization reduces redundant facts and update anomalies.

title: Indexes and write cost
short: Indexes accelerate reads but consume storage and add write maintenance.
answer: INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE may update several indexes. Use actual query plans to justify them.
code: CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer ON orders(customer_id);
interview: Indexes accelerate reads but consume storage and add write maintenance.

title: Composite index
short: A composite index contains multiple ordered columns; order matters.
answer: Design it around common predicates and sorting. It is not equivalent to separate single-column indexes.
code: CREATE INDEX idx ON orders(customer_id,status);
interview: A composite index contains multiple ordered columns; order matters.

title: WHERE vs HAVING
short: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters grouped results.
answer: Use WHERE to reduce input and HAVING for aggregate conditions.
code: SELECT dept,AVG(salary) FROM employee WHERE active=true GROUP BY dept HAVING AVG(salary)>70000;
interview: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters grouped results.

title: INNER vs LEFT JOIN
short: INNER keeps matches; LEFT keeps every left row.
answer: A WHERE predicate on the right table can turn a LEFT JOIN into an effective inner join.
code: SELECT c.id,o.id FROM customer c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id=c.id;
interview: INNER keeps matches; LEFT keeps every left row.

title: Window functions
short: They calculate across related rows without collapsing them.
answer: ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK, SUM OVER and LAG support analytics with row-level detail.
code: SELECT name,salary,DENSE_RANK() OVER(ORDER BY salary DESC) rnk FROM employee;
interview: They calculate across related rows without collapsing them.

title: Find duplicate email/contact
short: Group by both columns and filter count > 1.
answer: SELECT email,contact_number,COUNT(*) cnt FROM student GROUP BY email,contact_number HAVING COUNT(*)>1;
code: How return full duplicate rows?
interview: Group by both columns and filter count > 1.

title: Database transaction
short: A transaction groups database work with commit/rollback semantics.
answer: Transactions protect atomicity and consistency while isolation controls concurrency.
code: BEGIN; UPDATE account SET balance=balance-100 WHERE id=1; COMMIT;
interview: A transaction groups database work with commit/rollback semantics.

title: ACID
short: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation and Durability describe transaction guarantees.
answer: Atomicity is all-or-nothing; consistency preserves constraints; isolation controls concurrency; durability concerns committed data survival.
code: // debit + credit commit together
interview: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation and Durability describe transaction guarantees.

title: SQL deadlock
short: Transactions can wait cyclically for each other's locks.
answer: Databases may abort one transaction. Keep transactions short and use safe bounded retries.
code:
T1 locks A -> waits B
T2 locks B -> waits A
interview: Transactions can wait cyclically for each other's locks.

title: EXPLAIN / execution plan
short: It shows how the database plans to execute a query.
answer: Inspect scans, joins, indexes, row estimates and actual statistics where supported.
code: EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id=42;
interview: It shows how the database plans to execute a query.

title: DELETE vs TRUNCATE vs DROP
short: DELETE removes rows, TRUNCATE clears table contents as a bulk operation, DROP removes the table object.
answer: DELETE supports WHERE. Exact TRUNCATE behavior varies by database.
interview: DELETE removes rows, TRUNCATE clears table contents as a bulk operation, DROP removes the table object.

title: View vs materialized view
short: A normal view stores a query definition; a materialized view stores results.
answer: Materialized views trade freshness and refresh cost for faster reads.
code: CREATE VIEW active_customers AS SELECT id,name FROM customer WHERE active=true;
interview: A normal view stores a query definition; a materialized view stores results.

title: CTE
short: A CTE names a subquery for readable multi-step queries.
answer: WITH can support recursive queries where the DB allows them. Materialization is optimizer-dependent.
code: WITH high_salary AS (SELECT * FROM employee WHERE salary>80000) SELECT * FROM high_salary;
interview: A CTE names a subquery for readable multi-step queries.

title: Troubleshoot slow SQL
short: Inspect actual query, plan, indexes, locks, row counts and recent changes.
answer: Use EXPLAIN/EXPLAIN ANALYZE safely, inspect blocking and test targeted changes on realistic data.
code: slow query -> plan -> locks -> index -> re-test
interview: Inspect actual query, plan, indexes, locks, row counts and recent changes.

title: Transaction isolation
short: Isolation controls what concurrent transactions can observe.
answer: Isolation levels trade consistency and concurrency. Exact behavior is database-specific.
code: @Transactional(isolation=Isolation.READ_COMMITTED)
interview: Isolation controls what concurrent transactions can observe.

title: What is the N+1 query problem?
short: When fetching a list of N parent entities, and then lazily accessing an association on each one individually, Hibernate issues one query for the parents plus N additional queries (one per parent) to fetch each one's association — N+1 total
answer: When fetching a list of N parent entities, and then lazily accessing an association on each one individually, Hibernate issues one query for the parents plus N additional queries (one per parent) to fetch each one's association — N+1 total queries instead of one efficient join, badly hurting performance as N grows.
interview: When fetching a list of N parent entities, and then lazily accessing an association on each one individually, Hibernate issues one query for the parents plus N additional queries (one per parent) to fetch each one's association — N+1 total queries instead of one efficient join, badly hurting performance as N grows.

answer: JPQL queries entities and their properties/associations in an object-oriented, database-agnostic way, and JPA translates it to the appropriate SQL dialect. answer: An annotation used on Spring Data JPA repository methods to supply a custom JPQL (or, with \nativeQuery = true\, native SQL) query explicitly, instead of relying on Spring Data's method-name-derived query generation — useful for complex queries that don't map cleanly to a method name.

A non-clustered index is a separate structure holding pointers back to the actual rows, ordered independently of physical storage — a table can have many, useful for speeding up lookups on non-primary-key columns.

title: Explain `INNER JOIN`.
short: Returns only rows where there's a match in both joined tables based on the join condition — rows from either side without a corresponding match in the other are excluded from the result.
answer: Returns only rows where there's a match in both joined tables based on the join condition — rows from either side without a corresponding match in the other are excluded from the result.
interview: Returns only rows where there's a match in both joined tables based on the join condition — rows from either side without a corresponding match in the other are excluded from the result.

title: Explain `LEFT JOIN`.
short: Returns all rows from the left table, plus matching rows from the right table where they exist; if there's no match, the right table's columns are filled with NULL for that row.
answer: Returns all rows from the left table, plus matching rows from the right table where they exist; if there's no match, the right table's columns are filled with NULL for that row.
interview: Returns all rows from the left table, plus matching rows from the right table where they exist; if there's no match, the right table's columns are filled with NULL for that row.

title: Explain `RIGHT JOIN`.
short: Returns all rows from the right table, plus matching rows from the left table where they exist; unmatched left-table columns are filled with NULL. It's functionally equivalent to swapping the table order and using a LEFT JOIN.
answer: Returns all rows from the right table, plus matching rows from the left table where they exist; unmatched left-table columns are filled with NULL. It's functionally equivalent to swapping the table order and using a LEFT JOIN.
interview: Returns all rows from the right table, plus matching rows from the left table where they exist; unmatched left-table columns are filled with NULL. It's functionally equivalent to swapping the table order and using a LEFT JOIN.

title: Explain `FULL OUTER JOIN`.
short: Returns all rows from both tables — matched rows combined, and for rows with no match on either side, the missing side's columns are filled with NULL. Effectively the union of a LEFT JOIN and a RIGHT JOIN result.
answer: Returns all rows from both tables — matched rows combined, and for rows with no match on either side, the missing side's columns are filled with NULL. Effectively the union of a LEFT JOIN and a RIGHT JOIN result.

title: What is a self join?
short: A join of a table with itself, typically using table aliases to distinguish the two "copies" — used for comparing rows within the same table, e.g. finding employees and their managers where both are stored in the same employees table.
answer: A join of a table with itself, typically using table aliases to distinguish the two "copies" — used for comparing rows within the same table, e.g. finding employees and their managers where both are stored in the same employees table.

title: What is a cross join?
short: Produces the Cartesian product of two tables — every row from the first table paired with every row from the second, with no join condition. Result size is the product of both tables' row counts, so it's used deliberately (e.g. generating c
answer: Produces the Cartesian product of two tables — every row from the first table paired with every row from the second, with no join condition. Result size is the product of both tables' row counts, so it's used deliberately (e.g. generating combinations) rather than accidentally.
interview: Produces the Cartesian product of two tables — every row from the first table paired with every row from the second, with no join condition. Result size is the product of both tables' row counts, so it's used deliberately (e.g. generating combinations) rather than accidentally.

title: What is a subquery?
short: A query nested inside another query (in the SELECT list, FROM clause, or WHERE/HAVING condition), used to compute an intermediate result that the outer query then uses — e.g. filtering rows where a column is in the result set of a subquery.
answer: A query nested inside another query (in the SELECT list, FROM clause, or WHERE/HAVING condition), used to compute an intermediate result that the outer query then uses — e.g. filtering rows where a column is in the result set of a subquery.

answer: A subquery that references a column from the outer query, so it must be logically re-evaluated for each row processed by the outer query, rather than being computed once independently — e.g. finding employees whose salary is above the average salary of their specific department.
interview: A subquery that references a column from the outer query, so it must be logically re-evaluated for each row processed by the outer query, rather than being computed once independently — e.g. finding employees whose salary is above the average salary of their specific department.
